text: In 1919, Candler's family sold the company to a group of investors led by banker Ernest Woodruff. The price: twenty-five million dollars.
A few years later, his son Robert took over, and he ran Coca-Cola for decades. His goal was easy to say and hard to do: put a Coke within an arm's reach of desire.
That meant cartons that carried six bottles home. Coolers at gas stations. Vending machines. And ads everywhere, including the Christmas paintings of Santa Claus that started in 1931.
And no, Coca-Cola didn't invent the red Santa. He was wearing red long before that. But those ads made a warm, jolly Santa the one most people picture.
Then came World War Two. In 1941, Woodruff made a promise: every man in uniform would get a bottle of Coke for five cents, wherever he was... and whatever it cost the company.
To keep that promise, Coca-Cola shipped bottling equipment overseas. During the war, sixty-four bottling plants were set up, as close to the fighting as possible.
Millions of soldiers came home loving the drink. And the company came out of the war with a head start in dozens of countries. Coca-Cola went global by following the army.
